title: Plot an earthquake's waveform at an OOI seismometer, with the instrument response removed and a bandpass filter
summary: Gets an earthquake's record at one OOI seismometer from EarthScope, converts it from counts to ground velocity (or displacement or acceleration) by removing the instrument response, turns the horizontal components to true north and east, bandpass filters it, and plots each component against seconds after the origin time; it also writes the corrected traces as MiniSEED.
steps: Request the waveforms with a margin of PAD seconds on each side of the plotted window, and the station's response (level="response"); the margin is cut off at the end, so the taper and the filter's edges fall outside the plot.

Detrend and taper each trace, then remove the response with a pre-filter (pre_filt): four corner frequencies that taper the spectrum off outside the band where the instrument records ground motion, since dividing by its tiny response there would blow up noise. The script finds that band from each channel's own response: its low corner is the instrument's (about 1 Hz for the short-period CMG-6TF seismometers, 360 s for the broadband CMG-1T) or what the record's length can resolve, and its high corner is just below Nyquist. With pre_filt, the water level is turned off (water_level=None), as ObsPy's documentation advises.

With all three components, rotate the horizontals to true north and east (st.rotate("->ZNE", inventory=inv, components=("ZNE", "Z12", "123"))): the channels are named N and E, but some OOI seismometers' horizontals are not aligned with north, and their StationXML gives the azimuths. Without "ZNE" in components, ObsPy leaves channels named N and E as they are.

Bandpass filter for display (FREQMIN to FREQMAX, 4 corners, zero phase). This band is a choice for seeing the earthquake, separate from the pre-filter: Waldhauser et al. (2020) plot Axial microearthquakes at 4-50 Hz. Its top is kept below Nyquist (20 Hz on the 40 Hz B and S channels).
Trim to the window and plot each component against seconds after the origin time.
change: NETWORK and STATION for the station; CHANNELS stays None, so the script takes the station's fastest seismometer channels (HH? at a broadband station, EH? at a short-period one), unless the question names channels (? stands for every component, as BH?), ORIGIN for the earthquake's origin time (UTC; the Axial Seamount Earthquake Catalog gives Axial's), BEFORE and AFTER for the window, OUTPUT for ground velocity, displacement or acceleration, and FREQMIN and FREQMAX for the display band. Leave pre_filt to the script: it is computed from each channel's response.
pitfalls: A pre-filter or band above Nyquist fails: the 40 Hz B and S channels and the 8 Hz M channels need a lower FREQMAX (the script caps it at 0.45 of the sampling rate).
A short window cannot resolve a broadband seismometer's long periods: the script's pre-filter starts no lower than 2 divided by the record's length, so lengthen PAD to look at long-period motion.
One component alone (CHANNELS = "HHZ") is not rotated; rotation needs all three.

MiniSEED from EarthScope can have gaps, and its records can give the sampling rate a few parts per million off (200.00006 Hz), which stops ObsPy merging them; the script rounds the rate (moving samples by milliseconds at most) and fills gaps by interpolation, so a long gap plots as a straight line. A window inside a gap ends with "no data".
The HN channels (CMG-5T accelerometer) and HDH (hydrophone, in pascals) are other instruments at the broadband stations; HH, EH, SH and BH are the seismometers.

sources.title: Waldhauser et al. 2020, Precision Seismic Monitoring and Analysis at Axial Seamount Using a Real-Time Double-Difference System

title: Compute and plot a seismometer's noise power spectral density (PPSD) over days
summary: Gets one OOI seismometer channel from EarthScope a day at a time and computes its probabilistic power spectral density with ObsPy's PPSD (McNamara and Buland 2004): the instrument response removed, power in dB relative to 1 (m/s^2)^2/Hz in one-hour windows, plotted as the probability of each power at each frequency with the median and Peterson's 1993 low and high noise models, and as a spectrogram of how the power changed over the days; it also writes the median as a CSV table and the PPSD as an .npz file.
steps: Choose the channel: by default the station's fastest vertical seismometer channel (HHZ at a broadband station, EHZ at a short-period one), read from the station metadata.
Request one day at a time, so a long period never holds more than a day of 200 Hz data (about 70 MB) in memory; a day with no data is skipped.
Round each trace's sampling rate: EarthScope's records can give it a few parts per million off (200.00006 Hz), and PPSD skips a trace whose rate differs from the first.

Add each day to one PPSD built from the station's response (metadata=inv), which removes the instrument response itself; skip_on_gaps=True computes a PSD only where an hour has no gap, instead of filling the gap with zeros, which gives outlier PSDs.

Plot the PPSD against frequency with its median and Peterson's noise models, and the spectrogram of the hourly PSDs; write the median PSD as CSV and the PPSD as .npz, which PPSD.load_npz reads back to add more days.
change: NETWORK and STATION for the station; CHANNEL stays None for the fastest vertical seismometer channel, unless the question names one (a horizontal such as HHN, a slower band such as BHZ, or the hydrophone HDH at a broadband station, whose PSD is then in dB relative to 1 Pa^2/Hz); START for the first day and DAYS for how many (UTC); PPSD_LENGTH for the seconds in each PSD (longer resolves lower frequencies).
pitfalls: A seafloor seismometer's noise is not a land station's: at Hydrate Ridge and Slope Base the secondary microseism peak (0.14-0.2 Hz) is up to about 20 dB higher than at coastal stations, and below 0.03 Hz infragravity waves dominate the vertical (Hilmo and Wilcock 2020); expect the median above Peterson's low noise model there.

Below about 0.1 Hz the horizontals are dominated by tilt noise from seafloor currents, and the vertical by seafloor compliance near 0.02 Hz and by tilt (Crawford and Webb 2000): the horizontals are much noisier than the vertical at long periods.
The short-period CMG-6TF seismometers (EHZ) are flat only above about 1 Hz: their PSD below that is the response divided out of a small signal, and is not reliable at long periods.
One hour (PPSD_LENGTH = 3600) resolves down to about 0.003 Hz; the plot starts at ten times that.
Many days at 200 Hz take a while to download; for long periods a slower channel (BHZ, 40 Hz) is enough below 15 Hz.

sources.title: McNamara and Buland 2004, Ambient Noise Levels in the Continental United States
Peterson 1993, Observations and Modeling of Seismic Background Noise
Hilmo and Wilcock 2020, Physical Sources of High-Frequency Seismic Noise on Cascadia Initiative Ocean Bottom Seismometers
Crawford and Webb 2000, Identifying and Removing Tilt Noise from Low-Frequency Seafloor Vertical Seismic Data

title: Detect earthquakes with an STA/LTA coincidence trigger across OOI seismometers, and compare with the Axial catalog
summary: Gets the vertical channel of several OOI seismometers from EarthScope for a span of hours, bandpass filters them, runs a recursive STA/LTA (short-term over long-term average) on each, and counts a detection when enough stations trigger together (ObsPy's coincidence_trigger). It then reads the Axial Seamount Earthquake Catalog for the same hours and marks which detections are catalogued earthquakes; it writes the detections as CSV and plots them on one station's record with hourly counts beside the catalog's.
steps: For each station, take its fastest vertical seismometer channel (HHZ or EHZ) from the station metadata, request the span with a margin of three LTA windows before it, round the sampling rate (records can give it a few ppm off) and merge, filling gaps with zeros, which do not trigger.

Bandpass each trace. The default band, 35-80 Hz, lies above fin whale calls: on the recipe's test day (15 October 2025, six hours at Axial) a 7-50 Hz band gave 191 detections, nearly all of them fin whale calls (downsweeps from about 30 to 18 Hz every 23 s, on the seismometers and hydrophones alike), while 35-80 Hz gave 40, with 6 of the catalog's 7 earthquakes (magnitudes -0.1 to 0.7). Caplan-Auerbach et al. 2017 used 7-50 Hz for Axial microearthquakes, then screened out in-water sources such as whale calls.

Run the recursive STA/LTA (STA 0.2 s, LTA 10 s) on each trace and count a detection when MIN_STATIONS stations are above ON together, until they fall below OFF (coincidence_trigger); drop detections inside the margin, where the LTA is still settling.
Read the catalog's daily hypo71 files for the span and match each detection to an earthquake that began up to 3 s before it (P waves cross Axial's caldera in a second or two).
Write the detections (time, duration, stations, the matching catalog ID and magnitude) as CSV and plot them on the first station's filtered record, with detections and catalog earthquakes per hour.
change: STATIONS for the stations (OOI stations elsewhere, such as Hydrate Ridge's HYS11-HYS14 and HYSB1, work too, but the catalog comparison is Axial's only); START and HOURS for the span (UTC); FREQMIN and FREQMAX for the band; STA, LTA, ON, OFF and MIN_STATIONS for the trigger. Lower ON or MIN_STATIONS finds smaller earthquakes and more noise.
pitfalls: A band that includes about 15-35 Hz triggers on fin whale calls, which can outnumber earthquakes many times over; the 35-80 Hz default avoids them but loses some of the smallest earthquakes, and needs the 200 Hz channels.
A detection is not an earthquake: compare with the catalog, and look at the record. Detections not in the catalog may be earthquakes too small to locate, or noise.
One earthquake can give more than one detection a few seconds apart (later arrivals and reverberations); the CSV gives them the same catalog ID.
The catalog is the University of Washington's live Axial catalog of located earthquakes; its newest hours may not be located yet, and it covers Axial only.
Hours of 200 Hz data from seven stations take a minute or more to download; long spans are better run a day at a time.

sources.title: Caplan-Auerbach et al. 2017, Explosive processes during the 2015 eruption of Axial Seamount, as recorded by seafloor hydrophones

title: Plot a calibrated spectrogram of an OOI hydrophone, broadband or low-frequency
summary: Gets a span of an OOI hydrophone's record with OOIPy, the RCA's Python toolbox for its hydrophones: a broadband hydrophone (64 kHz) from the OOI raw-data archive, or a low-frequency one (200 Hz, at the broadband seismic stations) from EarthScope. It computes a spectrogram whose columns are Welch power spectral densities with median averaging, corrected by the hydrophone's frequency-dependent sensitivity from its calibration sheet, in dB relative to 1 uPa^2/Hz, plots it on a log frequency axis and writes it as NetCDF.
steps: Choose the hydrophone: a broadband one by its node (LJ03A Axial Base seafloor, PC03A Axial Base 200 m platform, LJ01A Oregon Slope Base seafloor, PC01A Slope Base 200 m platform, LJ01C Oregon Offshore, LJ01D Oregon Shelf), or a low-frequency one by its seismic station (AXBA1, AXCC1, AXEC2, HYS14, HYSB1).
Download the span with ooipy.get_acoustic_data (broadband, from the archive's 5-minute MiniSEED files) or ooipy.get_acoustic_data_LF (low-frequency, from EarthScope).

For a broadband hydrophone, find which hydrophone (asset ID) was deployed then in OOI's deployments list: OOIPy 1.3.0 does this itself, but fails for the hydrophone deployed now, whose end time is blank, so the script looks it up and gives it to OOIPy.

Compute the spectrogram with Welch's method and median averaging over AVERAGE seconds per column (data.compute_spectrogram): the median keeps the broadband hydrophones' ADCP pings from dominating, as Ragland et al. 2022 explain, and OOIPy applies the sensitivity correction, giving dB relative to 1 uPa^2/Hz.
Plot the asked frequencies on a log axis, with a colour scale spanning every frequency's typical level, and write the spectrogram as NetCDF.
change: HYDROPHONE for the hydrophone (a broadband node or a low-frequency station, as listed in the script), START and MINUTES for the span (UTC), FMIN and FMAX for the frequencies plotted; AVERAGE and L stay None unless the question asks for a time or frequency resolution (None gives 1 s and 3.9 Hz bins for a broadband hydrophone, 10 s and 0.39 Hz for a low-frequency one).
pitfalls: Broadband data are large: each 5-minute file is about 38 MB, so an hour is about 450 MB to download; for hours or days use the low-frequency hydrophones, or a longer AVERAGE on a few minutes at a time.
A low-frequency hydrophone samples at 200 Hz, so its spectrogram stops at 100 Hz; a broadband one's falls off above about 25 kHz, where the digitizer's anti-alias filter cuts in.
OOIPy 1.3.0 is pinned: the script works around its calibration lookup for the current deployment, which a later version may change.

Fin whale calls (about 18-30 Hz) fill the low-frequency band in autumn and winter; at 3.9 Hz bins a broadband spectrogram shows them only roughly, so use a low-frequency hydrophone or a larger L to see them.
A span spanning a gap in the archive returns less data or none; OOIPy merges what there is.

sources.title: Ragland et al. 2022, An overview of ambient sound using Ocean Observatories Initiative hydrophones

title: Compute and plot Axial Seamount's uplift (inflation) from the bottom pressure instruments, with uplift rates
summary: Reads OOI's daily mean seafloor depth (botsflu_daydepth, de-tided with the predicted tide) from ERDDAP for the bottom pressure and tilt instruments at the center of Axial's caldera (MJ03F) and on its eastern rim (MJ03E), turns each into uplift since the first day, and takes their difference: the differential uplift of the caldera center relative to the rim, which removes the tidal residuals and oceanographic pressure changes both stations share, as Oregon State University's Axial eruption forecasts use it. It fits uplift rates over the last 1, 3 and 6 months, plots both, and writes the daily uplift as CSV.
steps: Request only the rows that hold a daily depth (one a day): ERDDAP's constraint botsflu_daydepth!=NaN, added to the URL by hand because erddapy puts NaN in quotes, which ERDDAP refuses. A year is about 365 rows a station, so years come in one request.
Drop days whose QARTOD flag is 4 (FAIL) or 9 (MISSING), and keep the days both stations have.
Uplift is the change in depth from the first day (depths are negative, so rising makes them less negative), in cm; the differential uplift is the center's minus the rim's.
Leave out spike days, where one station's daily mean is tens of cm off: more than 6 robust standard deviations from the differential's 15-day running median.
Fit a straight line to the last 1, 3 and 6 months of each series for its rate in cm a year, and plot each station's uplift and the differential uplift with its rates.
change: START and END for the span (UTC); RATE_MONTHS for the months the rates are fitted over; CENTER and RIM for the stations (the ERDDAP dataset IDs of the Axial bottom pressure instruments: ooi-rs03ccal-mj03f-05-botpta301 Central Caldera, ooi-rs03ecal-mj03e-06-botpta302 Eastern Caldera, ooi-rs03int2-mj03d-06-botpta303 International District, ooi-rs03ashs-mj03b-09-botpta304 ASHES).
pitfalls: The differential uplift is smaller than the uplift at the caldera center, as the rim rises too: OSU's forecasts note a differential rate of about 10 cm/yr is equivalent to about 16 cm/yr at the center. On the recipe's test year (October 2024 to October 2025) the differential rate over the last 6 months was 9.7 cm/yr and the center's own 13.9 cm/yr.

A single station's de-tided depth keeps tidal residuals and oceanographic and barotropic pressure changes, so its rate over a month or two can be far off (over the last month of the test year, -20 cm/yr at the center); the differential removes what the stations share.
Pressure sensors drift; neither the differential nor the single-station uplift removes a drift of one sensor, which OSU checks with repeated ROV-based pressure measurements.
ERDDAP's International District data (MJ03D) end in July 2023, and each dataset ends where its newest data were processed; a span past the end returns fewer days.

botsflu_daydepth is OOI's product (from the 15-second bottom pressure means with the predicted tide removed); for the raw 20 Hz pressure use the Gold Copy's botpt_nano_sample stream from the instrument's download recipe.

sources.title: Eruption forecasts at Axial Seamount, Oregon State University
Plots of OOI Regional Cabled Array data, Oregon State University
OOI ERDDAP: Central Caldera bottom pressure and tilt
OOI ERDDAP: Eastern Caldera bottom pressure and tilt

title: Plot a shallow profiler's CTD as a depth-time section and a T-S diagram
summary: Reads a shallow profiler's CTD (temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen and pressure, with QARTOD flags) from OOI ERDDAP for a span of days, drops the values flagged as failed or missing, takes depth from pressure (TEOS-10), and plots each variable as a depth-time section of every sample, and a T-S diagram of absolute salinity and conservative temperature with potential density contours, coloured by depth; it writes the table as CSV.
steps: Request the CTD's pressure, temperature, salinity and oxygen with their QARTOD flags (*_qc_agg) for the span from ERDDAP; a week is about 30,000 rows, and months are better requested a month at a time.
Set a value flagged 4 (FAIL) or 9 (MISSING) to missing; 3 (SUSPECT) is kept, to judge on the plot.

Take depth from pressure with TEOS-10 (gsw.z_from_p): the dataset's own depth column is empty at Axial Base. If the depths span less than 20 m, the profiler was parked at its 200 m platform, not profiling, and the script says so.
Plot each variable at each sample's time and depth: the science pod profiles from about 200 m to about 5 m below the surface, nine profiles a day, as the RCA describes it.

Convert to absolute salinity and conservative temperature (gsw.SA_from_SP and gsw.CT_from_t, at the site's latitude and longitude) and plot them over contours of potential density anomaly (gsw.sigma0).
change: DATASET, LAT and LON for the profiler (ooi-rs01sbps-sf01a-2a-ctdpfa102 Slope Base, 44.53, -125.39; ooi-rs03axps-sf03a-2a-ctdpfa302 Axial Base, 45.83, -129.75); START and END for the span (UTC); VARIABLES for what to plot (any of the CTD dataset's variables in its download recipe, with a label).
pitfalls: The profiler is sometimes parked: at Axial Base it stayed at about 191 dbar from June to August 2025, so a section of those weeks is a single line; check the depths the script prints, or choose another span.
The dataset's depth column (depth_reading_profiler_depth_enabled) is empty at Axial Base; the script uses pressure instead.
The profiler's CTD dataset on ERDDAP is one row about every 19-30 s, not every sample; for every sample use the Gold Copy route in the CTD's download recipe.
A section of every sample shows the profiles as they were sampled, without gridding; gridding to regular depths and times smooths over the gaps between profiles.
TEOS-10 needs the site's position; a T-S diagram of practical salinity and in-situ temperature differs slightly from the one of absolute salinity and conservative temperature.

sources.title: OOI ERDDAP: Slope Base shallow profiler CTD
Off to the Races, Interactive Oceans

title: Plot an OOI instrument's time series without its QARTOD-failed samples, with daily (or hourly, weekly) means
summary: Reads one variable of any OOI ERDDAP dataset and its QARTOD flag (VARIABLE_qc_agg) a month at a time, counts the samples under each flag, drops those flagged as failed or missing, averages the rest over a period (daily by default) with their standard deviation, plots the samples kept, the samples dropped and the means, and writes the means as CSV.
steps: Request the variable and its aggregate QARTOD flag a month at a time: a dataset of a row a minute is about 44,000 rows a month, and one request of many months can time out; a month with no data (ERDDAP answers 404) is skipped.
Count the samples under each flag: 1 pass, 2 not evaluated, 3 interesting/unusual or suspect, 4 fail, 9 missing (OOI's Quality Control page).
Drop the samples whose flag is in DROP (4 and 9 by default); keep 3, which OOI uses for interesting or unusual data as well as suspect data.
Average what is kept over AVERAGE (pandas resample: 1D daily, 1h hourly, 7D weekly), with the standard deviation and the number of samples in each.
Plot the kept samples, the dropped ones in red and the means with their spread, scaling the axis to the kept samples, and write the means as CSV.
change: DATASET and VARIABLE for the instrument and what it measures (the instrument's download recipe lists its ERDDAP dataset ID and its variables with a QARTOD flag); START and END for the span (UTC); DROP for the flags to drop (add 3 to drop suspect data); AVERAGE for the averaging period.
pitfalls: Flag 3 is not only bad data: OOI uses it for interesting or unusual data too, which at a vent field or during an event can be the signal; on the recipe's test span (ASHES seafloor CTD temperature, January to June 2025) 28,686 of 258,626 samples were flagged 3 and none 4.
Flag 2 (not evaluated) means no test ran on that sample, not that it passed.
ERDDAP's OOI datasets are about one row a minute (some every 19-30 s), not every sample; for every sample use the Gold Copy route in the instrument's download recipe.
Only variables with a QARTOD test have a _qc_agg column; the instrument's download recipe says which.

A dataset ends where its newest data were processed, and some end years early on ERDDAP (the International District bottom pressure in July 2023): a span past the end returns no rows for those months.

sources.title: QARTOD Flag Statistics Using Cloud-Based Resources and Zarr Data Formats, OOI

title: Plot an ADCP's current speed and direction against depth and time
summary: Reads an OOI ADCP's eastward, northward and error velocity and its bin depths from its Gold Copy stream through OPeNDAP, leaves out samples whose error velocity is large, averages over an hour (or another period) per depth bin, blanking bins with too few good samples, computes speed and the direction the water flows toward, plots both against depth and time, and writes them as NetCDF.
steps: List the stream's Gold Copy files that overlap the span, keeping the ADCP's own files: its folder also holds the CTD files used to process it.

Read only the velocities, error velocity and bin depths for the span through OPeNDAP; OOI's east and north velocities are in Earth coordinates with the magnetic variation accounted for (the files' own description).
Leave out samples whose error velocity exceeds ERROR_MAX (0.1 m/s by default, a choice to tune): the error velocity measures how far the four beams disagree.

Average each file over AVERAGE (an hour by default; the Axial Base ADCP samples every second) and blank a bin whose share of good samples in the period is below MIN_GOOD, as far from the ADCP the echo is too weak: at Axial Base good hourly means reach about 220 m above the instrument.
Speed is the magnitude of east and north; direction is where the water flows toward, in degrees clockwise from north. Plot both against bin depth and time, with a cyclic colour map for direction.
change: DATASET for the ADCP's Gold Copy stream (its download recipe names the stream, such as RS03AXBS-LJ03A-10-ADCPTE303-streamed-adcp_velocity_beam at Axial Base); START and END for the span (UTC); AVERAGE for the averaging period; ERROR_MAX and MIN_GOOD for the screening.
pitfalls: A sample a second is about 86,400 rows of 50 bins a day: keep spans to days, or average longer; the script averages each file before combining.
Direction here is where the water goes (oceanographic convention), not where it comes from (as wind is given).
Bins far from the ADCP are noise: blank them (MIN_GOOD) rather than trusting their means.

A tidal current's direction turns through 360 degrees about twice a day near the seafloor at Axial Base; an hourly mean over a longer period averages the tide away, which is what a mean current needs.

Other ADCPs' streams have other names; use the stream the instrument's download recipe gives, and a stream without eastward_seawater_velocity (some give beam velocities only) does not work with this script.

sources.title: OOI Gold Copy: Axial Base ADCP stream

title: Find when OOI seismometers, hydrophones or other EarthScope channels have data, with daily availability, outages and gaps
summary: For OO network channels on EarthScope (seismometers, accelerometers, low-frequency hydrophones, BOTPT), finds when each channel was installed from the station metadata, the percent of each day it has data from EarthScope's MUSTANG quality metrics (or, for channels MUSTANG does not cover, by downloading each day), and writes a summary per channel (days with data, outages, longest outage, first and last day with data), the daily percents as CSV, a channel-by-day heatmap, and optionally every gap with its start and end.
steps: Get each channel's epochs (when it was installed) from the FDSN station service at level=channel, so a day without data is told apart from a day before the channel existed.

Get the daily percent_availability and num_gaps of every channel at once from EarthScope's MUSTANG measurements service (one row per channel per day, years in seconds). MUSTANG computes them only for seismometer and accelerometer channels, a day or two after the data arrive.

For channels MUSTANG has no metrics for (the hydrophone HDH, BOTPT pressure BDO and tilt LAX/LAY at location 11), or for every channel when LIST_GAPS is True, download each installed day from FDSN dataselect and measure it: the seconds with samples over 86,400, and each gap between records longer than MIN_GAP (ObsPy's get_gaps, before merging, plus the day's edges). MAX_DOWNLOAD_DAYS stops a span that would download too much: a day of a 200 Hz channel is about 25 MB.
Label each channel-day: not installed, no data (0 %), partial, full, or not computed yet (installed but MUSTANG has no value: its last day or two).
Summarise each channel and plot the daily percents as a channel-by-day heatmap (monthly means for spans over a year), grey where the channel was not installed or not computed.
change: STATIONS (a list or wildcards: AX* is Axial's, HYS* Hydrate Ridge's), CHANNELS (HHZ broadband and EHZ short-period seismometers; HN? the accelerometer; HDH the hydrophone; BDO the BOTPT pressure), START and END (days, UTC, END not included), LIST_GAPS = True with a span of days to list each gap, MIN_GAP for the shortest gap listed, MAX_DOWNLOAD_DAYS to allow a longer download.
pitfalls: EarthScope has retired its availability services: fdsnws/availability and irisws/timeseries answer "This service has been retired", and the station service refuses includeavailability and matchtimeseries (410 Gone), so scripts that use them fail; MUSTANG's metrics and the data themselves are what remain.

An open epoch in the station metadata does not mean data: the BOTPT channels at AXCC1, AXEC2 and AXID1 (location 11) are open, but their data on EarthScope end on 14 February 2024; the COSZO stations CZMID, CZOFF, CZOSH and CZSHF are listed from 22 August 2026 but had 0 % availability to 8 November 2026.
One instrument's availability is not another's at the same station: on 29 January 2025 AXCC1's seismometer (HHZ) missed three hours (87.5 %) while its hydrophone (HDH) recorded the whole day.

Outages often hit a whole node: Hydrate Ridge's HYS11, HYS12 and HYS14 had no data from 19 August 2020 to 9 August 2022, and HYSB1 had long outages in 2021 and 2023-2024; Axial's stations averaged about 95 % in 2025.
MUSTANG's last day or two are missing or partial and recomputed later; check the newest days again or download them.
BH, MH and LH channels are lower-rate copies of the HH and EH channels; ask for HH and EH to see what was recorded.

title: Find when an OOI instrument's variables have data on ERDDAP, day by day, with the gaps
summary: For any OOI instrument on the Data Explorer's ERDDAP (BOTPT, CTD, oxygen, ADCP ...), counts the values each of its variables has on each day in one request a year (ERDDAP's orderByCount), and writes a summary per variable (values in a full day, days with data, first and last day, gaps of MIN_GAP_DAYS or more), the gaps, the daily counts as CSV and a variable-by-day heatmap of the percent of a full day.
steps: Read the dataset's variables and units from ERDDAP's info page (dataset ID "ooi-" + the reference designator in lower case) and keep the measurements, not coordinates or QC flags.

Ask ERDDAP for the number of values each variable has on each day (orderByCount("time/1day") counts values that are not missing, per variable), a year at a time so a long record does not time out; a year with no rows answers 404 and is skipped.
Take a variable's usual count on a day with data (the median: 1440 for 1-minute data, 1 for a daily product) as a full day, and each day's count as a percent of it.
List each run of days without data at least MIN_GAP_DAYS long, and summarise each variable.
Plot the percents as a variable-by-day heatmap (monthly means for spans over a year and a half).
change: REFDES for the instrument (its download recipe gives the reference designator and ERDDAP dataset); keep VARIABLES = None, which counts every variable of the dataset, so the one asked about is there whatever its ERDDAP name (a CTD's oxygen is moles_of_oxygen_per_unit_mass_in_sea_water); START and END (days, UTC, END not included; None is today); MIN_GAP_DAYS for the shortest gap listed.
pitfalls: ERDDAP answers a span without data with rows of NaN, not with nothing, so count the values, not the rows: Axial's caldera-centre BOTPT (RS03CCAL-MJ03F-05-BOTPTA301) has raw pressure (botpres) only from 11 August 2025 (Eastern Caldera and ASHES from 10 August 2025; International District 2014 to September 2022), while its de-tided depth (botsflu_meandepth) and tilt run from 2014.

Variables of one instrument have different gaps: the caldera-centre BOTPT's de-tided depth and tilt stop from 26 February to 21 June 2026 while its raw pressure continues; Axial Base's CTD (RS03AXBS-LJ03A-12-CTDPFB301) has depth_reading only from 11 August to 22 October 2025 in 2024-2025, while its temperature, salinity and pressure cover 99.5 % of days.
A model's prediction is not data: predtide and botsflu_predtide are tide predictions and are present on days the sensor recorded nothing.
Values present are not values that passed QC: the QC time-series task recipe drops QARTOD-failed samples.
ERDDAP's OOI datasets are about one value a minute; a day with all 1440 can still have gaps shorter than a minute in the full-rate data on the Gold Copy.

title: Save the waveforms of a list of earthquakes at several OOI seismometers, response removed and rotated to radial and transverse, with a record section
summary: Takes earthquakes from the USGS catalogue (anywhere in the world), the Axial Seamount Earthquake Catalog or a list of origin times, and for each event and station downloads a window around the predicted P arrival, removes the instrument response, rotates the horizontals to true north and east and then to radial and transverse, and saves MiniSEED, StationXML and SAC files with the event and station in the SAC header, a table of what was saved for each event and station (or why not), and a record section of the vertical components by distance.
steps: Get the events: USGS ComCat's largest MAX_EVENTS in QUERY, within REGION's radius of its point when set, or the Axial catalogue's daily hypo71 files (latitude and longitude in degrees and minutes, west), or EVENTS as a list of origin times with their location when known.

For each station, compute the distance, azimuth and back azimuth to the event and the predicted first P arrival in the iasp91 model (ObsPy TauP); with no location, the window is set from the origin time and the horizontals stay north and east.

Pick the channels: at each station its slowest seismometer channels sampled at MIN_RATE or more (BH or SH at 40 Hz for distant events, HH or EH at 200 Hz for local ones with MIN_RATE = 100), unless CHANNELS names them.

Download BEFORE to AFTER seconds around P with PAD seconds more each side, merge (rates rounded, short gaps filled and counted), detrend, taper, and remove the response with a pre-filter from each channel's own response and no water level.

With three components, rotate to true north and east with the metadata's azimuths, then to radial and transverse with the back azimuth (ZRT); filter a copy of the vertical for the record section, then cut everything to the window; a station with less than 90 % of the window is reported as incomplete.

Save per event: MiniSEED and StationXML per station, a SAC file per component with stla, stlo, evla, evlo, evdp, mag, gcarc, az, baz, the origin (o) and P (a) in its header, and the record section; and the table of every event and station.
change: CATALOG and QUERY for the events (starttime, endtime, minmagnitude), and REGION for where (latitude, longitude and a radius in degrees: the script's comment gives the Blanco fracture zone, Axial's caldera and Mendocino; None is the whole world, so a question naming a place needs REGION), or EVENTS for your own list; MAX_EVENTS; STATIONS; MIN_RATE (20 for distant events, 100 for local ones) or CHANNELS; BEFORE and AFTER around P; OUTPUT; FREQMIN and FREQMAX for the record section only (the saved traces are not filtered).
pitfalls: Predicted P is a model's time, not a pick: for the M8.8 Kamchatka earthquake of 29 July 2025 the onset showed 1 s after iasp91 P at the quiet land station IU.ANMO but 13 s after it at AXCC1 and 19 s at HYSB1 (0.5-2 Hz), as the rupture's weak start is hidden in seafloor noise; Axial microearthquakes arrive 0.2-0.4 s after iasp91 P, as the shallow crust is slower than the model.
At Axial's caldera (about 1,520 m deep) arrivals about 2.0 and 4.1 s after P on every station are the sea surface's reflections (twice the water depth at 1.5 km/s), not S waves or more earthquakes.

Short-period stations (AXAS1, AXAS2, AXEC1, AXEC3, AXID1, HYS11-13, CMG-6TF with a 1 s corner) do not record long periods: the pre-filter keeps their records above about 0.5 Hz, so a distant event's surface waves are seen properly only on the broadbands (AXBA1, AXCC1, AXEC2, HYS14, HYSB1).
Rotation to radial and transverse needs all three components and the event's location; a station with one component, or an event with only an origin time, stays in Z, N and E.
The OO stations had long outages (Hydrate Ridge from August 2020 to August 2022): a station with no data or an incomplete window is listed in events_stations.csv rather than saved.
USGS ComCat returns the largest MAX_EVENTS of the search, which for a great earthquake's days are its aftershocks too; narrow QUERY or raise minmagnitude.

sources.title: USGS ComCat FDSN event web service
Kennett and Engdahl 1991, Traveltimes for global earthquake location and phase identification

title: Remove the tides from an Axial BOTPT's bottom pressure and get the seafloor's depth change, hour by hour
summary: Reads an Axial bottom pressure and tilt instrument's 15-second mean pressure from OOI's Gold Copy over OPeNDAP (only the span is downloaded, for any date since 2014), converts it to depth with TEOS-10, fits the tides to a year of hourly depths with UTide and takes the daily and faster ones away, also low-passes the depth with a Godin filter, compares both with OOI's own de-tided depth, and writes hourly CSV, the tidal constituents and a plot, with the depth trend.
steps: List the Gold Copy THREDDS folder REFDES-streamed-botpt_nano_sample_15sec and open, over OPeNDAP, the files whose time span overlaps the year before END (or the span asked for, if longer), reading only botsflu_meanpres (15-s mean pressure, psi) and OOI's botsflu_meandepth for those times.

Convert to sea pressure (psi to dbar, less one standard atmosphere, as the gauge reads absolute pressure) and to depth with TEOS-10 (gsw.z_from_p) at the site's latitude; average hourly, keeping hours with at least half their 240 means.

Fit the tides with UTide (ordinary least squares, with a linear trend so uplift does not leak into the tides) to FIT_DAYS of hourly depths ending at END: a year separates K1 from P1 and S2 from K2, which are 182 days apart in beat.

Predict the daily and faster constituents over the span asked for and subtract them; the fortnightly, monthly and seasonal constituents stay in the residual, as they are as much ocean and volcano as tide.
Low-pass the hourly depth with a Godin filter (24, 24 and 25-hour running means) as a check that needs no tide model, and compare with OOI's BOTSFLU de-tided depth.

Report the tide left in each de-tided series (rms about a 2-day running mean), the largest constituents and the trend over the span and over the fit's year; write the hourly series, the constituents and the plot.
change: REFDES for the site (RS03CCAL-MJ03F-05-BOTPTA301 caldera centre, RS03ECAL-MJ03E-06-BOTPTA302 eastern rim, RS03INT2-MJ03D-06-BOTPTA303 International District, RS03ASHS-MJ03B-09-BOTPTA304 ASHES), START and END (UTC, END not included), FIT_DAYS for the tide's fit (keep a year), GODIN.
pitfalls: Each route covers different years: EarthScope's 20 Hz pressure (OO.AXCC1, AXEC2, AXID1 location 11, BDO) ends on 14 February 2024; ERDDAP's 1-minute botpres has the caldera centre, eastern rim and ASHES only from August 2025 and the International District only to September 2022, and ERDDAP's de-tided depth and tilt stop from 26 February to 21 June 2026. The Gold Copy's 15-s product covered every day of 2024 and 2025 at the caldera centre, and the International District through March 2026.

A tide fitted to less than about six months leaves the K1-P1 beat behind: at the caldera centre, a fit to January-March 2025 left 8.4 cm rms of tide, a fit to the year before 1.6 cm; one-month fits give K1 phases from 218 to 250 degrees as P1 hides in K1, while M2's stayed within a degree, so the clock is not to blame.

A month's trend is mostly ocean: at the International District, March 2026 gave +29 cm/yr while the year to it gave -9.4 cm/yr; for uplift use months to years, or the differential uplift of the Axial uplift task recipe, which cancels what the ocean does to both sites.
A single gauge's trend includes its own drift, which only campaign pressure measurements at the same benchmarks can correct.
The Godin filter loses the first and last 35 hours, and it takes away everything faster than about two days, not only tides.
Depth here is from TEOS-10 sea pressure; OOI's BOTSFLU depth uses its own conversion and tide model, so compare their changes, not their levels.

sources.title: Codiga 2011, Unified Tidal Analysis and Prediction Using the UTide Matlab Functions
Nooner and Chadwick 2016, Inflation-predictable behavior and co-eruption deformation at Axial Seamount

title: List an OOI seismic station's channels, epochs, orientations and instrument responses, and explain them
summary: Reads the StationXML of OO network stations from EarthScope at the response level and writes a table of every channel epoch (what each channel code means, sampling rate, azimuth and dip, sensor and datalogger, sensitivity with its frequency and units, units per count, the band within 3 dB of flat, and the response's stages), checks that each sensor's two horizontals are 90 degrees apart, explains how counts become physical units, and plots each kind of channel's response.
steps: Request the stations' channels at level=response from EarthScope's FDSN station service, for every epoch or for one TIME.

For each channel epoch, decode its SEED code (band: sampling rate and broadband or short-period; instrument: seismometer H, accelerometer N, pressure D, temperature K, tilt A; orientation) and read its azimuth, dip, sensor, datalogger and overall sensitivity (counts per input unit at a stated frequency).

Compute the response's amplitude over frequency and find where it is within 3 dB of its largest value: the band where dividing by the sensitivity gives the physical value; outside it the full response must be removed.
List each stage (poles and zeros, gain, FIR) with its gain, and write the table as CSV.
Check each sensor's two horizontals (N and E, or 1 and 2) are 90 degrees apart, and flag those that are not.
Plot one channel of each kind's latest response (amplitude divided by sensitivity, and phase) against frequency.
change: STATIONS (a list or wildcards), CHANNELS (EarthScope takes * and ? and comma lists, not [ ] ranges), LOCATION ("" for seismometers and hydrophone, 11 for the BOTPT channels), TIME for the metadata at one time.
pitfalls: HYS11's metadata gives EHN an azimuth of 0 and EHE 125 degrees, which are not at right angles (HYS12 and HYS13 nearby give 35 and 125), so one is wrong and rotating HYS11 with them gives wrong north and east; the script flags it.

Some horizontals are turned from north: AXEC1's EHN points 128 and EHE 218 degrees, AXEC3's 35 and 125, and HYS12's and HYS13's 35 and 125; channels named N and E must be rotated with their azimuths (ObsPy's Stream.rotate with the inventory and components including ZNE).

The low-frequency hydrophones' (HDH) metadata response is flat down to 0.0001 Hz, but the hydrophone is not: at AXCC1 on 1 June 2023, HDH converted with it gave the microseism (0.2-0.3 Hz, coherence 0.95-0.98 with the BOTPT pressure gauge) at 0.1-0.3 % of the gauge's pressure, so HDH pressures below a few hertz are far too small.

The BOTPT pressure channel (location 11, BDO) holds float32 psi, not digitiser counts: its sensitivity, 1.45038e-4 per Pa, is 1/6894.757, so dividing by it gives pascals; its data on EarthScope end on 14 February 2024. Its tilt (LAX, LAY in microradians) and temperature (BK1, in C) are in their units already, with a sensitivity of 1.

Most OO channels have one epoch from 2014 to now; HYS13's have three (new on 25 June 2019 and 21 August 2022), each with its own sensitivity, so remove the response with the epoch covering the data's time (ObsPy does when given the inventory).
The sensitivity is exact only at its frequency; a broadband record's long periods (below its 360 s corner) and every record near Nyquist need the full response removed, with a pre-filter.

title: Read the RCA's fibre-optic DAS data (2021 OptaSense, 2024 and 2025 OptoDAS) and convert it to strain or strain rate
summary: Finds the PI data portal's DAS files for a span of time (the 2021 OptaSense community test on the north or south cable, the 2024 OptoDAS, or the 2025-26 OptoDAS on the south cable), downloads each whole, keeps a range of distance along the fibre, converts the 2021 phase to strain and the OptoDAS phase rate to strain rate with each file's own header values, joins the files and checks for gaps, integrates or differentiates to the output asked for, band-passes, optionally removes the common mode, flags dead and noisy channels against their neighbours, and writes a NetCDF (with each 2021 channel's latitude, longitude and water depth from the portal's geometry file), a channel table and a waterfall plot.
steps: List the portal folders for the span: das/data/Optasense/{North,South}Cable/{TransmitFiber,ReceiveFiber}/<run>/ (one-minute files named with their UTC start), das24/data/YYYYMMDD/dphi/hhmmss.hdf5 (10 s), or das25/data/OptoDAS/YYYY/MM/DD/south/8Hz/ (10 s); a file runs until the next starts.
Download each file whole (the portal ignores byte ranges) and read only the channels between DIST_KM, then delete it.

2021 OptaSense (ProdML): RawData [locus, time] is phase in 2 pi / 2^16 rad; strain = phase x 1550 nm / (4 pi n xi G) with n the file's refractive index (1.4682), xi = 0.78 and G its GaugeLength (Lindsey et al. 2020); times are RawDataTime in microseconds.
OptoDAS: data [time, channel] is phase rate per metre; strain rate = data x header/dataScale / header/sensitivities (rad per strain per metre); channel distances are cableSpec/sensorDistances.

Join the files; where one ends more than a sample before the next starts, filter and integrate each stretch apart. Strain from strain rate is integrated only after joining (cumulative trapezoid); strain rate from strain is its time derivative.
Band-pass (zero-phase Butterworth) to BAND; report the share of variance common to all channels at each instant and, with COMMON_MODE, subtract the median across channels.
Flag channels whose rms is a tenth (dead) or three times (noisy) that of the 51 around them, and save the NetCDF, the channel table and a distance-time waterfall.
change: EXPERIMENT (das2021, das24 or das25), CABLE and FIBER (das2021 only), START and END (UTC, END not included), DIST_KM (optical distance from the interrogator, km), CHANNEL_STEP, OUTPUT (strain_rate or strain), BAND (Hz, or None), COMMON_MODE, MAX_FILES (a guard on the download).
pitfalls: The portal sends whole files only: a 2021 OptaSense minute is about 1.2 GB however few channels are kept, a 2024 OptoDAS 10-s file 76 MB and a 2025 8-Hz file about 2 MB; MAX_FILES stops a span from downloading more than intended.

The 2021 OptaSense files hold phase, not phase rate: so converted, their microseism strain (0.1-1 Hz, 20-40 km on the south cable, 1 November 2021) was 2.4e-8, against 1.9e-8 from the 2024 OptoDAS on the same cable. Their gauge length is 51.05 m (the GaugeLength attribute; the folder names say GL50m) and channels are 2.04 m apart.

In the OptoDAS headers dx (1.021 m) is before the region-of-interest decimation (roiDec 10): channels are 10.21 m apart, as cableSpec/sensorDistances gives; the gauge length is 40.85 m. The 2024 files hold float32 with dataScale 1, the 2025 files int16 with dataScale 7.51e-5; the script uses each file's own values.

The 2025-26 OptoDAS is public at 8 Hz only. Its authors report calibration problems: data at 40 m gauge length are the most reliable, and best just after a parameter change; it was down from 27 November to 5 December 2025, ran 25 m and 12 m gauge lengths from 16 December 2025 to 6 January 2026, and stopped on 28 January 2026.

The 2025-26 Nokia multi-span files (das25/MultiDAS) are a different, custom binary format of about 525 MB each, at 7.45 Hz or slower, and this script does not read them; their timestamps lag real time by about 7 s at 7.45 Hz and 12-13 s at 3.73 Hz (the authors' notes). The authors' notebook computes channel spacing with a fixed 4 that is the pulse count: with each file's Npulses it gives 52.9 m for a December 2025 file and 105.9 m for a 5 November 2025 one, as their table lists.

Distances are optical distance from the interrogator on shore, not position: for 2021 the portal's geometry file gives each channel's latitude, longitude and elevation (south channels 942-47381), so 30-60 km of the south cable lies in 216-542 m of water; no channel positions are published for the OptoDAS.

Each 2021 run has its own settings: the long 200 Hz runs cover the south cable from 1 November 23:11 to 5 November 14:06 UTC and the north cable from 3 November 22:08 to 5 November 14:06, the receive fibres only 5 November 14:20-17:00; the south run of 4 November is split into part1 and part2 folders that fill each other's gaps.

Fin whale calls (14-30 Hz) cross the south cable between 30 and 60 km at 07:16 UTC on 2 November 2021, as Wilcock et al. 2023 described; a channel flag against all channels would mark those carrying calls as noisy, so the script compares each with its neighbours.

sources.title: Lindsey et al. 2020, On the Broadband Instrument Response of Fiber-Optic DAS Arrays
Wilcock et al. 2023, Rapid: A Community Test of Distributed Acoustic Sensing on the OOI Regional Cabled Array
Lipovsky, Williams et al. 2024, RAPID: Multiplexed Distributed Acoustic Sensing at the OOI Regional Cabled Array
Dienstfrey, Lipovsky, Wilcock and Krauss 2026, Multi-span DAS on the OOI RCA 2025-2026: OptoDAS data
Krauss et al. 2026, Distributed Acoustic Sensing Beyond Optical Repeaters Offshore Oregon
uwfiberlab OOI_DAS_2025: reading the OptoDAS and multi-span data
Wilcock, Abadi and Lipovsky 2023, Distributed acoustic sensing recordings of low-frequency whale calls and ship noise offshore Central Oregon

title: Get an Axial BOTPT's seafloor tilt (LILY), with its relevels and steps taken out, as east and north
summary: Reads an Axial BOTPT's LILY tilt (x, y, corrected compass, temperature and QARTOD) from its Gold Copy files over OPeNDAP, one sample a minute, drops samples at the instrument's range, finds the relevels (the LILY driving itself back to level), sudden steps and jumps across gaps, takes those chosen out of the record after them, rotates x and y to east and north with OOI's corrected compass, averages hourly or daily, reports the tilt change over the span, and plots the recorded and stitched tilt and its path.
steps: List the botpt_lily_sample Gold Copy files overlapping the span and read lily_x_tilt, lily_y_tilt, corrected_compass_direction, lily_temp and the tilt magnitude's QARTOD result, one 1-Hz sample in every STEP (60), through OPeNDAP; skip and name files the server cannot read.
Drop samples beyond 329.9 microradians: the LILY reads +-330 at most.
After each gap of over an hour, drop the samples until the LILY's temperature is back within WARMUP (0.1 C) of the hour before the gap: it restarts cold and its tilt is off while it warms.

Find each step: a change of more than JUMP (10 microradians) between samples under an hour apart, or of more than GAP_JUMP across a longer gap; its size is the change from the hour before to the hour after. A relevel ends with x and y near zero; a step does not.
Take the kinds in REMOVE out of everything after them, dropping the samples during each.

Rotate x and y to east and north with the median corrected compass (y's bearing; x is 90 degrees clockwise), which reproduces OOI's seafloor_tilt_direction; average, and report the change from the first to the last day.
change: REFDES (RS03ECAL-MJ03E-06-BOTPTA302 eastern caldera, RS03CCAL-MJ03F-05-BOTPTA301 caldera centre, RS03INT2-MJ03D-06-BOTPTA303 International District, RS03ASHS-MJ03B-09-BOTPTA304 ASHES), START and END (UTC, END not included), STEP (seconds between samples read), AVERAGE, JUMP and GAP_JUMP, REMOVE, WARMUP.
pitfalls: ERDDAP's tilt (one value a minute) holds International District only to 22 July 2023, and every site misses 26 February to 21 June 2026 (and 9 May to 1 June 2020, 27 November to 14 December 2023); the Gold Copy's 1-Hz LILY files run from 2014 to now at all four sites.

Relevels: the LILY sends nothing for 4-10 minutes and comes back with x and y near zero, and not only near its +-330 microradian range (eastern caldera 21 May 2018 from -300 and -125; International District 13 February 2024 from 211 and 118, and 23 July 2026 from 57 and 48). Hourly means mix the two levels, so steps are found in the minute samples.

After an outage the LILY restarts cold (unpowered, it cools ~1.5 C) and its tilt is 15-25 microradians off, the same way each time at a site, coming back over ~12 hours as it warms; taken as offsets across the gaps, the caldera centre's outages of 2023-2024 added 206 microradians toward 211 degrees to a change of 63 toward 92. The script drops the warm-up (WARMUP) before looking for jumps across a gap.

The eastern caldera LILY also jumped 12-72 microradians within a minute without relevelling on 29 April 2016, 8 November 2016, 4 March 2017, 26 March 2019 and 14 April 2019, none within 3 minutes of an earthquake in the Axial catalog; the script takes them out by default (REMOVE). An eruption tilts the ground hundreds of microradians in hours, as in April 2015: look at the step list before removing them then.

x and y are the instrument's own axes. OOI's corrected compass (ion-functions prs_bottilt_ccmp, a per-sensor lookup on the LILY's compass) gives y's bearing: 195 degrees at the eastern caldera, 106 at International District. ERDDAP gives it from -180 to 180 (-165 for 195), and its raw compass as bottilt_scmp.

Direction: with x, y and the corrected compass, OOI's seafloor_tilt_direction is (450 - atan2(y, x) + ccmp) mod 360. As Axial reinflated, the stitched tilt moved 218 microradians toward 82 degrees at the eastern caldera (2016-2019, the jump across the June 2016 file gap taken out) and 297 toward 161 at International District (2023 to October 2026), both within 45 degrees of directly away from the caldera centre (MJ03F lies at 302 and 323 degrees from them).

Some Gold Copy LILY files fail on the server (DAP error 500, java.io.EOFException), leaving gaps, among them: eastern caldera 8 June-4 July 2016, 18 April-14 May 2017, 9 June-5 July 2017 and 21 September-17 October 2017, International District 22 July-17 August 2025, caldera centre 12 January-8 February 2025; a relevel inside such a gap is found as a jump across it.

sources.title: OOI ion-functions: BOTPT tilt products, prs_functions.py
Nooner and Chadwick 2016, Inflation-predictable behavior and co-eruption deformation at Axial Seamount
Chadwick et al. 2022, Geodetic Monitoring at Axial Seamount Since Its 2015 Eruption

title: Get a seafloor point current meter's (VEL3D: MAVS or Vector) currents, cleaned, with tides and subtidal flow
summary: Reads an RCA seafloor point current meter (MAVS-4 at Axial and Hydrate Ridge, Nortek Vector at the Oregon Shelf and Offshore benthic packages) from its Gold Copy files over OPeNDAP, one sample every few seconds, drops QARTOD-failed samples, impossible speeds, low-correlation Vector samples and garbled MAVS records, averages hourly with a coverage rule, and reports the mean flow, speed, principal axis, tidal constituents (UTide) and subtidal flow, with a plot of speed, components, the velocity cloud and a progressive vector diagram.
steps: List the Gold Copy files of the instrument's stream overlapping the span (vel3d_b_sample for a MAVS, vel3d_cd_velocity_data for a Vector, whose folder also holds system_data files) and read east, north and up velocity with their QARTOD results, plus beam values (and MAVS pitch and roll), one sample every SAMPLE_SECONDS.

Drop a sample if any velocity has a QARTOD flag in DROP or exceeds MAX_SPEED, if a Vector beam correlation is below MIN_CORRELATION, or if a MAVS beam is railed or its pitch or roll is more than MAX_TILT_CHANGE from the median.
Average over AVERAGE, blanking periods with under MIN_SHARE of their samples; speed and the direction the water flows toward.

Principal axis from the hourly velocity covariance; UTide fitted to hourly u and v (15 days or more) for the tidal ellipses and the share of variance that is tidal; subtidal flow from a Godin 24-24-25 h low-pass, bridging gaps of up to 6 hours.
change: REFDES (RS03INT2-MJ03D-12-VEL3DB304, RS03AXBS-MJ03A-12-VEL3DB301, RS01SUM1-LJ01B-12-VEL3DB104, RS01SLBS-MJ01A-12-VEL3DB101, CE02SHBP-LJ01D-07-VEL3DC108, CE04OSBP-LJ01C-07-VEL3DC107), START and END (UTC, END not included), SAMPLE_SECONDS, AVERAGE, DROP, MAX_SPEED, MIN_CORRELATION, MAX_TILT_CHANGE, MIN_SHARE.
pitfalls: ERDDAP's Vector velocities (the Oregon Shelf and Offshore VEL3D-C) are 10 times too large through 26 November 2023: OOI's code divides by 10 when bit 1 of the Vector's status code says its units are 0.1 mm/s, and ERDDAP's values are exactly 10 times the Gold Copy's on 1 March 2016 and 31 December 2022 (Offshore) and 1 March 2018 (Shelf). From 19 December 2023 the two agree (1 March 2025). Read the Gold Copy, as this script does.

ERDDAP's MAVS (VEL3D-B) northward velocity is the raw magnetic-frame north while its eastward velocity is corrected for declination: on 10 October 2023 at Southern Hydrate Ridge ERDDAP gave north -10.2 cm/s, the raw value, where the Gold Copy's rotated north was -7.2 cm/s; east agreed. The Gold Copy's pair is a true rotation of the raw one.

A MAVS can fail with QARTOD passing: at Southern Hydrate Ridge in September and October 2023 a beam railed near -32316 counts with pitch and roll jumping from about 2 and 4 to -27.5 and 28.6 degrees in 29,352 of 405,618 samples, and others read 14.128 m/s; uncleaned, hourly means reached 80 cm/s against a 95th percentile of 12 cm/s once cleaned.

Vector samples with a beam correlation under 70 % were 16 % of January 2023 at Oregon Offshore; median near-bed speed there was 7.2 cm/s, at International District 1.2 cm/s (January-February 2025) and at Southern Hydrate Ridge 6.2 cm/s (September-October 2023).

The Gold Copy holds the Oregon Shelf Vector from 2014 to now; ERDDAP's copy ends on 19 March 2024. The deep profilers' current meters (VEL3D-A) are other datasets, with velocities named _profiler_depth_enabled, and this script does not read them.
Direction is where the water goes. A month of hourly means separates M2 from S2 but not K1 from P1, which needs about a year (UTide warns of the Rayleigh criterion).
Some Gold Copy files fail on the server (DAP error 500), such as the Oregon Offshore Vector's of 1-2 January 2023; the script names them and goes on.

sources.title: OOI ion-functions: velocity products and nortek_scale_velocity, vel_functions.py
Codiga 2011, Unified Tidal Analysis and Prediction Using the UTide Matlab Functions

title: Find which of the ASHES diffuse-flow thermistors are in warm water, and how their temperature follows the tide
summary: Reads the ASHES diffuse-flow temperature array (24 thermistors, a value a minute) from ERDDAP with QARTOD flags, a month at a time, drops flagged values, averages hourly, compares each probe with the ambient seawater from the CTD on the same junction box, reports coverage, flags, stuck runs and which probes are warm, fits the tides (UTide) to the warm probes and to the bottom pressure beside them (Gold Copy 15-s means) to give each constituent's lag after the pressure, and plots the probes with the ambient.
steps: Request tempsfl_01 to tempsfl_24 and their _qc_agg flags from ERDDAP a month at a time, and drop values flagged in DROP.
Hourly means (blank with under half the minutes); the ambient is the CTD's hourly mean sea_water_temperature (ERDDAP orderByMean).
Per probe: coverage, flagged and stuck minutes (one value repeated FLAT_MINUTES or more), median, 95th percentile, maximum, and median excess over the ambient; warm if the excess is over WARM.

For 15 days or more: UTide on each warm probe's hourly temperature and on the BOTPT's hourly pressure from the Gold Copy's 15-s means; each constituent's lag is the phase difference converted to hours (positive: the temperature peaks after the pressure).
change: START and END (UTC, END not included), AVERAGE, DROP, WARM (C above ambient), FLAT_MINUTES; DATASET, CTD and BOTPT are the ASHES array, CTD and pressure gauge.
pitfalls: Which probes are warm changes over the years (daily means): probe 2 read 17-27 C from October 2014 to June 2015, and 43-67 C from 18 June to 13 August 2017 while probe 6 read 42-114 C from 26 January to 13 August 2017, when no other probe passed 9.1 C (check such values before using them); probe 7 read about 6.5-12.6 C from mid-2018 to May 2021. Since 2022 no probe's yearly mean has been above 3.4 C, against 2.4-2.7 C for the coldest probe.

The CTD on the junction box reads 0.1-0.2 C colder than the coldest probes (March 2019: 2.41 C against 2.48-2.55 C), so WARM is 0.5 C: in March 2019 probes 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 14 were warm, probe 7 the warmest at a median of 9.9 C.

In March 2019 the diurnal tides (O1, K1) in probes 1 and 5 were as large as or larger than M2 (probe 5: O1 0.28, K1 0.23, M2 0.21 C), although the pressure's M2 (0.78 dbar) is over twice its K1 (0.31); a month cannot separate K1 from P1 or S2 from K2, so treat the diurnal and semidiurnal bands rather than single constituents.
ERDDAP's TMPSF rows are one a minute with 49 columns: a year is about 525,000 rows, so the script asks a month at a time.
ERDDAP's ASHES bottom pressure (botpres) begins only in August 2025; the pressure tide comes from the Gold Copy's 15-s BOTSFLU means, as in the BOTPT detide recipe.

sources.title: Mittelstaedt et al. 2016, Diffuse venting at the ASHES hydrothermal field: heat flux and tidally modulated flow variability
OOI ERDDAP: ASHES diffuse vent fluid temperature array
